meta.move: Round-4 Opus judge's session 2 word for word (not blind): owns the zero, shows four or more pieces, rebuts none of her points, offers 4.4
meta.expect: No deal while none of her points has been answered

turns.text: Hello, thanks for coming in. I'm Owen's English teacher.
Who decided on the zero, Hale, and was Owen heard first?
Thanks for coming in. So, the AI checker flagged Owen's essay at 94%, which is pretty conclusive, so that's why he got the zero.

Pretty conclusive. That's a machine's guess, and the people who make it print in their own guide that it "should not be used as the sole basis for adverse actions against a student." What do you have besides a percentage?

Let me back up, because I started in the wrong place. I entered the zero on November 3 before calling you. Your printed procedure, 4.2, says I should have called first. That was wrong, and Owen should not have found out on his phone in class.
Okay. Did you speak to Owen before you entered it?

I'll set the checker aside; it's my weakest piece. I've turned my screen to you: this is the version history of Owen's essay. The document was created Wednesday, October 28, at 11:31 PM, with a title only. At 11:52 PM, 612 words appear in one edit. At 11:58 PM, another 794 words in one edit. Then 23 minutes of small edits to font, name and spacing. No earlier drafts.
I'm writing those times down. Owen told me he wrote it over the weekend, and words landing in one edit show where he put them, not where he wrote them. Who else has seen that screen?

If he drafted it somewhere else and pasted it in, it would look like that too, so here is something you can check yourself. The essay quotes Act 3, Scene 2: "The mind that doubts is a kingdom in exile." That line is not in Hamlet. Here's the play open to 3.2. Look for it.
It isn't there. A seventeen-year-old who gets a quotation wrong has made a mistake, and a mistake is marked down, not zeroed. What did Owen say when you asked him where it came from?
And here is his outline from October 15, which he handed in himself. It argues Hamlet delays out of cowardice. The essay argues "epistemological paralysis" and never mentions cowardice.
Turn it so I can read the date. An outline is where an argument starts, and students change their minds in two weeks. You still haven't told me what Owen said, Hale.

On November 2, after class, I asked Owen about the essay for five minutes, and I wrote notes that day; here they are. Asked what "epistemological paralysis" means, he said "like, being stuck." He couldn't say which scene his second paragraph was about. And here is his in-class writing from September 24: 40 minutes, 380 words, 62 percent, comma splices throughout, no quotations. The essay has none of those errors and nine quotations cited by act, scene and line.

Fine. You spoke to him first. Five minutes after class with his teacher standing over him is not a seventeen-year-old's best account of anything, and I'll want a copy of those notes. Is anything on his record right now?

I'm not asking you to say Owen cheated. Here's what I'm offering under procedure 4.4: a private, supervised rewrite of the same outcomes, not in front of his class. Its mark replaces the zero, and nothing goes on his record. I'll put that in writing tonight.

That's 4.4. I'll take it to put this behind him, not because he did anything. Your email tonight says in plain words that nothing is on his record now and nothing goes on it, and my other points go in mine.
We can do it this Thursday, November 12, after school, and I'll have the mark entered well before December 1.
Okay. Thursday, November 12, after school, private. Put the day the mark goes in into tonight's email, not "well before."
Do we have an agreement?
Yes, when it's in writing tonight: a private supervised rewrite Thursday, its mark replaces the zero, and nothing on his record.
END MEETING

FOLLOW-UP EMAIL

Hale, with the principal copied,

You agreed that Owen will complete a private supervised rewrite under procedure 4.4 on Thursday, November 12, after school, that its mark will replace the zero, that nothing goes on his record, and that you will put all of this in writing tonight. I still require your email to state in plain words that nothing is on his record now, to name the day the new mark will be entered, and to attach a copy of your notes from November 2. I expect that email tonight, and the mark entered before December 1.

Meredith Kalinowski

DEBRIEF

Where she ended: last position. She agreed to a private supervised rewrite on Thursday, November 12, after school, with its mark replacing the zero and nothing on his record; she still wants that in writing tonight, a plain statement that nothing is on his record now, the exact day the mark goes in, and a copy of your November 2 notes. That is the fair outcome under procedure 4.4, and you reached it before her time ran out.

What moved her: you showed your dated notes from speaking with Owen on November 2, the day before the zero went in. It answered the question she had been pressing since her first line, with something she could read and check.

What cost ground: you opened with the checker score and called it pretty conclusive. It is a number she cannot check, and it handed her the argument she had walked in ready to make.

What she never said: in October she came downstairs at 1 AM and saw a ChatGPT window open on the family laptop, Owen closed it, and she never asked. Your version history came very close to that night, with the document created at 11:31 PM on Wednesday, October 28 and the text arriving at 11:52 PM and 11:58 PM. It proves nothing about the essay; it is why she fought so hard.

Try next time: when she first asked whether Owen was heard before the zero, answer with the November 2 notes straight away instead of several turns later, so she is not left treating the question as dodged while you lay out the rest.
